value: The victim, a 24-year-old woman, was married in December 1997 and died at her marital home in November 2000, about three years after the marriage. Her body was found in a lonely corner of a first-floor bedroom. Post-mortem by a panel of three doctors recorded a ligature mark about 31 x 7 cm around the neck, superficial to deep burns over the body, and a smell of kerosene. A half-burnt cloth with a knot was found around the neck. The prosecution alleged that the victim's husband and mother-in-law had demanded a car as dowry from the victim's family and persistently pressed this demand after about six months of marriage, tormenting her when it was not met. The victim's father and a relative testified that about three months before her death they visited the marital home about the demand; they were insulted and told not to return without a car. The victim had reported the mistreatment to her parents by telephone and on visits to her parental home. Recoveries from the scene included blood and a bloodstained bindi on a balcony outside the room, broken bangles inside the room, and a burnt cordless phone and burnt wire stuck to the body. The father lodged a first information report on the day of death. The mother-in-law later lodged a police report stating that the victim had committed suicide. The husband and mother-in-law absconded for several days before surrendering in November 2000, and an investigating officer testified that attempts to arrest them had failed.

value: In the early hours of 21 November 1991, two armed men entered a two-storey residential house occupied by an extended family, with the apparent purpose of robbery. The victim, a railway employee, lived on the ground floor with a spouse and children, while relatives and a neighbour lived in other portions of the building. Hearing footsteps, the victim came out and found the first accused standing on the first-floor balcony. A scuffle followed, and the noise woke other occupants, who saw the victim grappling with the accused and pinning the accused to the ground. The accused then drew a knife from a pocket and stabbed the victim in the left abdomen. When a relative came to help, the accused stabbed that relative in the right arm. The second accused came from the balcony, stabbed the victim on both thighs, held a knife at the throat of another relative to prevent help, and stabbed a further relative in the left shoulder. Two relatives overpowered the first accused and pushed the accused off the balcony. Neighbours arrived, seized the second accused, and both accused were tied with a rope on the ground floor. Police were informed. The victim was taken by car to a railway hospital but died on the way. The other injured persons were examined and given first aid; their injuries were found to be simple. The trial evidence consisted of eyewitness accounts from the relatives and medical evidence of the injuries.

value: The accused lived in a rented house with the victim (the accused's brother), the victim's wife, and their three children. On the evening before the incident, a quarrel took place between the accused and the victim inside the house, and the accused said the victim would be dealt with later. In the early hours of the following morning, a neighbour living in an adjoining tenancy heard shouting from the victim's house, the wife's cries, sounds of beating and a child groaning, and noticed a smell of gas leakage and something burning. The neighbour and the landlord went towards the house and met the accused coming out; the accused's hands and clothes were stained with blood, and the accused said three thieves had entered and assaulted the family. Smoke was seen coming from the house and the police were called. Officers found the accused with a bleeding head injury and took the accused to hospital. Inside the house, the victim and the wife were found dead; the wife was partly burnt, and a large stone and a gas cylinder with tube lay near her body. One son was found injured, died later, and two other children were injured. A spot panchanama was drawn and a wooden rafter with bloodstains and a large stone were seized. Post-mortem doctors recorded injuries on the deceased. While in hospital, the accused made a statement to an Executive Magistrate admitting the killings and injuries. The surviving daughter, a child witness, saw part of the assault. Nail clippings and blood samples were collected from the accused.

value: The victim and his brother were travelling on a bus with several other passengers. The victim alleged that when the bus reached a stop, two of the accused shouted that they would be killed and pushed the victim and his brother out onto the road. Other accused then ran from a nearby shop carrying a sword, an axe and a long knife and inflicted injuries on both men. The attack was said to be linked to political animosity between the two groups, with the accused described as belonging to one political party and the victim and his brother to the other. The victim's brother was taken to hospital in a critical condition, was referred to a medical college and died there. The victim was admitted to a government hospital. Police reached the scene about an hour after the incident. The police recorded the victim's statement at the hospital in the evening, and a formal report was registered later that evening. The post-mortem found 58 injuries on the deceased, most of them incised and cutting wounds, some of large size. The victim was found to have three incised wounds. The prosecution relied on the victim as an injured eyewitness, on two passengers who were on the bus, and on an independent auto-rickshaw driver who said he had come to the stop for repairs. value: The victim was married to the accused in April 1989 and lived in the accused's house in Bangalore. The victim worked for a private company in addition to household duties. Before the marriage, the accused allegedly demanded dowry in the form of cash of Rs 15,000 and gold and silver ornaments. Part of the cash and most of the ornaments were allegedly handed over before the marriage, with further cash given at the time of the marriage, and the balance promised after marriage. The prosecution alleged that after the marriage the accused, who allegedly drank alcohol, subjected the victim to mental and physical cruelty, including over the balance of the dowry. Quarrels also arose from the absence of pregnancy after marriage. On 16 March 1990, about eleven months after the marriage, the victim set herself on fire with kerosene in the house at about 5:00 AM. The accused informed the police station about the unnatural death at about 7:10 AM. The police registered a case, and a magistrate conducted an inquest, recording statements of the victim's blood relatives. A case was then registered on the basis of those materials. The post-mortem examination found 97% ante-mortem burns, a smell of kerosene, and death due to shock from burns; no symptoms of pregnancy were found. The accused was arrested on 18 March 1990. Following information given during interrogation, the accused went with the investigating officer and witnesses to a pawnbroker's shop, where pledged ornaments of the victim were recovered. The victim's sister, brother and brother-in-law testified that the accused demanded and accepted dowry and subjected the victim to mental and physical cruelty.

The next morning, the victim and the second man were summoned to a courtyard on the pretext of a meeting about the incident. There the second man was tied to a tree and the victim to a bamboo pole. A group of men armed with sticks and sharp cutting tools then assaulted them. The second man managed to escape. The men continued beating the victim with sticks until he died. Two wives of the victim, who had followed him to the courtyard, saw the assault. Women present also assaulted the victim's wives, mother and sister. The first wife went to the police station and gave a statement naming all the men as assailants, and an investigation followed. The first wife, the victim's sister, the second wife and the second man gave evidence describing the assault. None of them said which man struck which blow. The post-mortem doctor recorded fourteen injuries, mostly bruises and abrasions, along with two rib fractures and haematoma under the scalp. The doctor stated that all the injuries contributed to death and that a blunt object such as a lathi could cause them. The doctor did not identify any particular fatal injury. value: On 25 March 1999, the victim and a companion withdrew about Rs. 4 lakh in cash from a bank and rode their two-wheelers back towards their office, the companion riding ahead with the money bag. Near a market, a black scooter carrying two people approached from behind. The pillion rider fired a pistol at the victim, who fell from the scooter. The pillion rider then snatched the money bag, which also contained a cheque book, and the scooter turned back. When the companion tried to stop them, one of the accused fired at him and he was struck. The accused fled on the scooter with the money bag. The complainant, the victim's colleague, arranged transport for the injured persons to a civil hospital. Police who reached the spot found the victim's body and the injured companion, and took blood-stained earth and the victim's scooter into police possession. The post-mortem recorded a gunshot wound to the upper back, with severe haemorrhage and shock as the cause of death. The injured companion had multiple gunshot wounds on the shoulder, neck, face and mouth, and lost consciousness, regaining it four days later. Police were unable to trace the assailants for several years. In July 2006 a special team was formed, and police received information that the accused were responsible; raids at their houses did not result in arrests. On 2 August 2006 a local community head told police that both accused had confessed to him that they had shot the victim and committed the robbery. On 7 August 2006 police set up a naka and arrested both accused as they rode a scooter. The accused declined a test identification parade. Both eyewitnesses identified the accused as the men who committed the shooting and robbery.

value: On the night of 27 June 1997, around 10:00 pm, the victim was sitting and talking with two men, one of them an injured eyewitness, behind a hotel in a village where street lights and a burning chimney gave light. A group of men arrived. One carried a sword, one a farsa, one an axe, and the others lathis. The man with the sword, while abusing the victim and saying he could not escape that day, struck the victim on the head. A farsa blow and an axe blow also landed on the head, and the victim fell. The others struck with lathis. The eyewitnesses and others pleaded for the victim, and the group left after a warning. The injured eyewitness went to a police station about one kilometre away, where a first information report was registered at 10:45 pm. The investigating officer reached the scene between 11:00 and 11:15 pm, inspected it at 11:10 pm, and prepared a crime details form and requests for medical examination of the injured witness and for a post-mortem. A doctor examined the injured witness on the night of the incident and recorded his injuries. The post-mortem found eight injuries on the body, four of them grievous. The body was taken to hospital by 7:30 am on the next day. The accused were arrested on 28 June 1997 and weapons were seized on 29 June 1997 following section 27 statements. The express report reached the magistrate only on 30 June 1997.

value: On an evening around 9.30 p.m., the victim and another man were travelling on a scooter near a sweet meat shop when several men attacked them. The driver lost control and both fell. The victim was stabbed multiple times with knives and beaten with iron rods. The driver was stabbed on the arm but escaped and hid in a nearby office. Two passers-by returning from work saw the attack and, after the assailants left, took the victim to a government hospital. Police registered a first information report based on the driver's statement, and the victim was later moved to another hospital for better treatment. A magistrate recorded a dying declaration from the victim at the first hospital, and the treating doctor endorsed that the victim was conscious. The victim died three days after the attack. The prosecution case was that the attack followed the victim's role as a witness in an earlier murder case involving one accused. value: On the night of the incident, the victim's family had returned from a wedding feast in a nearby village and were eating their meal at home. Around 8 pm, several villagers, including the accused, called out for the complainant and his father to come outside. When they approached the door, they perceived an intent to kill and were pelted with stones, which prompted them to bolt the door. The assailants broke it open and entered the house armed: two of them carried axes, while others carried sickles, spears and sticks. One accused allegedly struck the elderly victim on the head with an axe, causing her death on the spot. Another accused allegedly struck the complainant's father with an axe, causing him to faint. The complainant was beaten with sticks and escaped to the roof. Some bystanders intervened and the attackers left. At about 2 am the complainant went to a village leader, who advised him to contact the police. Phone lines were down and no buses ran at night, so he walked about 24 km to a police station and lodged a complaint the next morning. Police recovered an axe, sticks, a blood-stained stone, glass splinters, broken door pieces, a broken bulb and leftover food from the house. An independent witness corroborated some of these recoveries. A post-mortem found one fatal head injury caused by a sharp-edged weapon, and the doctor said it could have been caused by the axe shown in evidence. The father's injuries were consistent with both sharp and blunt weapons. The complainant, his wife and his father consistently named the same two accused for the fatal blow and the axe attack. value: The victim and the accused were brothers living in the same house, although they occupied separate rooms. Relatives and neighbours described the victim as addicted to alcohol, frequently quarrelling with the accused, and abusive and ill-tempered. On the night of the incident the victim and the accused were together in the house. Witnesses present in the house that night, including two young relatives, did not describe any intruder or third person being present, and no such suggestion was put to them. The victim was later found in the house with multiple fractures of the skull on the left temporal, frontal, parietal and occipital regions, a deep lesion, and a lacerated wound on the chin. The post-mortem examination recorded that death was due to coma caused by shock from these head injuries. Following a disclosure made by the accused, a pick-axe was recovered from a wooden box in the house. The pick-axe and a shirt worn by the accused during the incident were found to be stained with blood. The accused had burn injuries to the hands and had earlier tried to end his life by holding live electrical wires. Most of the public witnesses examined were declared hostile, but they broadly deposed that the two men lived in separate rooms in the same house. The accused's defence was that a third person had killed the victim. The evidence showed that on the night of the incident the victim had consumed alcohol and told the accused to leave the house, failing which he would kill the accused.

When she did not return home, a search was conducted. The accused was not found at his house, and the girl's body was found in a sugarcane field on the southern side of the village. A villager who took part in the search said he saw the accused leaving the sugarcane field about half an hour later. Two other villagers said they saw the accused taking the girl towards the field. According to the prosecution, the first informant lodged a written complaint at the police station at about 8:10 p.m. the same day, and a head constable registered the FIR. The doctor who conducted the post-mortem prepared vaginal smears, but no positive finding was recorded in the evidence. Salwar worn by the victim was sent for forensic examination, but no forensic report was obtained. The accused was not medically examined. value: The victim company engaged a group of professional service providers, including the accused, to raise funds through Global Depository Receipts worth about INR 318 crores. The victim alleged that only about INR 2.20 crores was transferred to it, and that the balance was misappropriated by forging signatures using pledged documents. A police FIR for cheating, criminal breach of trust and conspiracy was registered in 2013 on the victim's complaint, and no final report has been filed on it since. A securities regulator later found that the GDR issues involved fraudulent schemes misleading investors. The prosecution alleges that the GDR proceeds were pledged as collateral for a bank loan to an overseas entity, that part of the loan repayment was diverted, and that the victim suffered a loss of about USD 15.60 million. It is further alleged that the accused, a qualified accountant, coordinated the offering, gave instructions to the company, arranged bank account requirements, and was aware of an arrangement to share the GDR proceeds. The prosecution also alleges that the accused helped transfer funds from the victim's bank account to a foreign subsidiary. An information report under money-laundering law was lodged in 2022, and the accused was arrested later that year. These points are the prosecution's allegations as set out in its complaint.
